alternative: Build the dependency first in a constructor function and pass it to the embedded type's own constructor (NewStream(buf)) or set it in the composite literal; where the outer value must be reachable from the inner one, pass an explicit back-pointer or an interface. Go embedding is composition - the Book of Go explicitly says it does not provide subclassing - so no base-before-member order exists that would need re-ordering trickery.
idiom_name: embedded struct initialised by the constructor function (no base list, no ordering rule)
implementation_notes: Go has no inheritance at all: embedding a type borrows its methods - and when those methods run, the receiver is the inner value, not the outer one - so there is no base subobject whose initialisation must precede the rest, and no base-specifier list to order. What replaces the classic structure is the constructor function and the composite literal: build the payload first, then hand it to the embedded type's own constructor or place it in the literal, and the order is simply the order you write. There is nothing to encapsulate with a helper type, and the classic form has no Go counterpart; the only surviving part of the pattern's motivation is identity - if the inner value needs the outer one, Go requires an explicit back-pointer or an interface, since embedded methods never dispatch to the outer type.
pitfalls: Embedded methods dispatch on the inner value: a method inherited from the embedded type can never see the outer value's other fields, so any dependency in that direction must be passed in explicitly - Go has no virtual dispatch to fall back on.

A back-pointer into the outer value (or a pointer to one of its fields) makes the value non-copyable in practice: copying the struct duplicates the payload while the pointer keeps aiming at the original, with no compiler complaint.
Struct literals are the initialisation mechanism, so ordering invariants live only in the constructor function's body; a caller that builds the struct literal directly bypasses them.
